# Welcome {.unnumbered}

::: {.lead}
This is a practical guide to PLINK for people who work with livestock SNP data. You do not need to be a programmer. If you can type a command and read a table, you can follow every chapter.
:::

I wrote this tutorial because most PLINK material is written for human genetics. The ideas are the same in cattle, sheep and goats, but the details are not: we have 29 cattle autosomes instead of 22, we have big half-sib families, we mix breeds, and our pedigrees are often wrong. Every example here uses livestock data, and every output you see was produced by actually running the command shown.

## How this book works

Each chapter follows the same rhythm:

1. **The idea**, in plain words, usually with a picture.
2. **The command**, ready to copy.
3. **The real output**, exactly as PLINK printed it.
4. **What it means**, and what you should do next.

Boxes like the one below give extra help along the way.

::: {.callout-tip}
## Tip
Green boxes give practical advice that saves time.
:::

::: {.callout-note}
## PLINK 2.0
Blue boxes show how to do the same thing in PLINK 2.0.
:::

::: {.callout-warning}
## Common mistake
Orange boxes point out traps that catch almost everyone at least once.
:::

## What you will learn

| Part | Chapters | You will be able to |
|---|---|---|
| Getting started | 1 to 4 | Install PLINK, run it from the terminal and from RStudio, understand the file formats |
| Managing data | 5 | Convert, subset, merge and fix files |
| Quality control | 6 to 8 | Remove bad SNPs and bad samples, and explain why |
| Relationships and structure | 9 to 11 | Measure LD, relatedness and inbreeding, and run and read a PCA |
| Association analysis | 12 to 16 | Run case/control, quantitative, family, haplotype, CNV, epistasis and meta-analyses |
| Putting it together | 17 to 19 | Choose thresholds, analyse real cattle and sheep data, and run a full QC pipeline |

## The data

We use two kinds of data.

**A simulated cattle dataset** (361 animals of three breeds, 4,800 SNPs). Because it was simulated, we know the truth: I hid lab errors (bad samples, a duplicate, a wrong sire, sex mix-ups, strand flips) and real genetic effects in it, and the chapters show how PLINK finds each one.

**Two real public datasets**: 500 genotyped cattle with a pedigree (from the synbreedData R package) and 100 sheep of two breeds, Jacob and Navajo-Churro, published by Kijas and colleagues (2016) and shipped with the detectRUNS R package. These show what real data look like, which is always a little messier than a simulation.

Everything is in the [`data/`](https://github.com/Megaluno/PLINK_Tutorial/tree/main/data) and [`scripts/`](https://github.com/Megaluno/PLINK_Tutorial/tree/main/scripts) folders of the GitHub repository, so you can repeat every step.

## Which PLINK?

PLINK has three versions that are still in use. This book uses **PLINK 1.9** for almost everything, gives the **PLINK 2.0** command in a blue box, and uses **PLINK 1.07** only for the old tools that newer versions dropped (haplotype tests and CNV analysis). Chapter 1 explains the differences.
